material: Old growth western red cedar and copper domes
locationOnSite: front entrance of the building
description:
The Musqueam House Boards - Eagles & Salmon was commissioned by Vancouver Coastal Health Authority (VCH) as part of their participation in the City of Vancouver's Public Art Program for Private Development.

The Musqueam House Boards - Eagle & Salmon is one of two artworks commissioned for this location. The Musqueam Male & Female Welcome Figures were also a part of this project.
statement:
"The House Boards are carved from a red-cedar log; their design is of eagles and salmon. Since the Musqueam have always lived in and around the Fraser River, we thought it would be powerful to show the abundance of eagles and salmon that lined the trees and shores of this area. The Eagle is a renowned symbol of great significance and sends messages and prayers to the Creator. If an Eagle is seen during a Prayer session, it's a sign of having a prayer accepted; If a prayer needs immediate attention from the Creator, an eagle feather is held up towards the sky.

The gift the Eagle shares is the ability of foresight and an indication of good times to come; feathers are also symbolic gifts to impart respect for accomplishment and display of courage and wisdom.

The importance of salmon to the northwest coast is integral. They are the sustenance that the Musqueam people have relied upon for thousands of years. They bring people together in friendship and in marriages from far away villages. They represent renewal and prosperity."

title: B6 Public Art Screen
description: The building features a long curved façade and this curve is echoed within the lobby. This forms a curving feature wall which can be seen from many different viewpoints inside and outside the building. This curved wall is the location of the public art media installation. The art wall length is approximately 35 feet and a height of approximately 11 feet, and has expansive views from West Pender and Thurlow Streets. The curve of the screen is intended to create an animated artwork to engage the viewer passing through the lobby. Given the flexibility in presenting one or more programs, the curve is an element that captures public attention and engages their attention. A single program may be sown in this “zone” or the site specific artwork may be expressed across the whole surface. The idea is that the audience does not see everything all at once, but are invited to explore the presentation.

title: We Have Forgotten but They Have Not
locationOnSite: At the open public courtyard space fronting Oak Street
description: The artwork consists of a granite boulder, which was salvaged from the work site for its dimensions, pleasing surface finish and quality. The bronze elements were selected fromspecific animals insects and flora. (Salish Wooley Dog, Extinct,)(Phrynosoma Douglasi Pygmy Short Horned Lizard Last confirmed sighting 1910,) (Cicindela Parowana, Parowana Tiger Beetle South Okanagan, last confirmed sighting 1953,)  (Eremophila Alpestris Strigata Horned Lark Strigata subspeices, Lower Fraser Valley, last confirmed sighting 1987,) and the (Pseudephemerum nitidum, Delicate Earth Moss.)
statement: The intention of my project is to raise the awareness of history, landscape and species in this region.Based on the official website of the Government of British Columbia under Wildlife in BC at Risk provided online, I have selected a variety of species to be included in the sculpture. Perhaps this boulders can be viewed as a reminder of the fragility of our environment to local residents and others who will encounter this artwork. I’m hoping that the work can generate dialogue on the idea of preserving and protecting species that exist today.

title: Syewá:l (Ancestors) house post
locationOnSite: South corner of plaza
description:
Syewá:l (Ancestors) is a house post commissioned through our Public Art Program, in partnership with Vancouver Civic Theatres. It is located at šxʷƛ̓exən Xwtl’a7shn, the plaza outside the Queen Elizabeth Theatre.

It was created as part of the Artist-Initiated Program, which invites artists to propose their own public artworks and sites.
statement:
For səlilwətaɬ (Tsleil-Waututh) artist Zac George, his house post titled Syewá:l—meaning “Ancestors”—embodies the deep-rooted relationship between the local Nations and the Robson Street corridor, an area historically used for hunting and food gathering. The work also reflects his personal lineage.

The post honours his grandfather, the late Chief Dan George, who is portrayed toward its base, just above a traditional Coast Salish weaving pattern.

At the top sits a carved takaya (wolf) face, symbolizing the Tsleil-Waututh people having descended from the Wolf Clan, while the figure beneath it pays tribute to the women and grandmothers in his ancestry.

title: Blanketing
locationOnSite: Atrium
description:
Six large-scale vinyl banners, each with a full colour photograph depicting hand-made blankets in various locations and conditions.

Platforms: The Teachers Among Us invited emerging and mid-career artists to nominate senior artists who have mentored, taught, or profoundly influenced their artistic journey. Following a citywide nomination and adjudication process, 20 senior artists were selected to create new works to be showcases across civic art platforms. These pieces reflect the importance of mentorship and the intergenerational relationships that helped shape Vancouver’s vibrant art scene.
statement: The banners and zine that make up the work Blanketing are reflections on an abundance of textile hand work. There is intention and creativity in both the creating and maintenance of blankets (quilts, comforters, duvets, throws, crib blankets, and more). As objects with organic and inorganic components, blankets lead active lives, warming bodies and then carrying evidence of those lives in their shape, smells, stains, mends, and eventually discarded fibers. The six banners show blankets that are part of the creative legacy of my mother, who passed last year, my late grandmothers, and other unknown makers. I have mended and transformed them into clothing. In every banner there is a silhouette drawing of a bed with stacked blankets. It is also on the cover of the zine Blanketing that is available in the VPL Zine collection near the entrance to the library (level 2). The six images are set in the rural Pacific Northwest. They were photographed by Carl Wiebe and me on Malcolm Island, in the traditional Kwakwaka'wakw territories of the 'Namgis, Mamalilikala, and Kwakuitl Nations.

title: Wolf
locationOnSite: West facing window on Cambie Street
description: Platforms: The Teachers Among Us invited emerging and mid-career artists to nominate senior artists who have mentored, taught, or profoundly influenced their artistic journey. Following a citywide nomination and adjudication process, 20 senior artists were selected to create new works to be showcases across civic art platforms. These pieces reflect the importance of mentorship and the intergenerational relationships that helped shape Vancouver’s vibrant art scene.
statement: Wolf is a large-scale photograph of a carved tool handle. The image highlights the deep connection between Coast Salish artistry and the tools that sustain it. The identifying information — my name, the title, and description — appears directly on the photograph, integrating context into the artwork itself. In this way, the piece speaks both visually and textually, affirming that Musqueam art is inseparable from its makers, stories, and traditions.

title: Sitting Bull in Vancouver
description:
Site-specific vinyl wrap installation on an internally illuminated structure. The work features portraits of Sitting Bull alongside re-articulation of his speeches.

Platforms: The Teachers Among Us invited emerging and mid-career artists to nominate senior artists who have mentored, taught, or profoundly influenced their artistic journey. Following a citywide nomination and adjudication process, 20 senior artists were selected to create new works to be showcases across civic art platforms. These pieces reflect the importance of mentorship and the intergenerational relationships that helped shape Vancouver’s vibrant art scene.
statement: As one of the greatest spiritual and political leaders of the Lakota people – I am forever grateful for Sitting Bull’s wisdom and spiritual practice. He was deeply committed to Lakota people living and continuing culture under great duress during his lifetime. He scarified so the people may live. This work situates his nobility, striking appearance and fortitude within an urban setting. I have re-articulated a few sentences from his public speeches to hopefully inspire all to hear and see deeply and in the profundity of seeing and hearing, may we hear and see each other in good ways that inspire each other to walk gently.

title: Landmark (Sequoia Symbiosis)
locationOnSite: South facing windows
description: Platforms: The Teachers Among Us invited emerging and mid-career artists to nominate senior artists who have mentored, taught, or profoundly influenced their artistic journey. Following a citywide nomination and adjudication process, 20 senior artists were selected to create new works to be showcases across civic art platforms. These pieces reflect the importance of mentorship and the intergenerational relationships that helped shape Vancouver’s vibrant art scene.
statement: The work is a translucent collage of images of Coast Salish / Vancouver landmarks, including north shore mountains (the Sisters), sequoia trees on Cambie Boulevard, views from Lighthouse Park, etc. The artist's intention is to mirror the immediate site and its wider geographical context, and in particular to suggest relationships between culture and nature, revealing the symbiosis of the city with its natural environment.

title: Gentle Reminders
locationOnSite: Window of plaza entrance to skytrain station
description: Platforms: The Teachers Among Us invited emerging and mid-career artists to nominate senior artists who have mentored, taught, or profoundly influenced their artistic journey. Following a citywide nomination and adjudication process, 20 senior artists were selected to create new works to be showcases across civic art platforms. These pieces reflect the importance of mentorship and the intergenerational relationships that helped shape Vancouver’s vibrant art scene.
statement:
Gratitude is a state of mind
Love over money
what you see in others exists in you
sometimes progress does not look like progress
Ubiquitous, sometimes pithy , sometimes game changers. Always polite - attempting to keep things on track- optimistic and annoying.Positive intentions mixed in with cognitive dissonance.

These drawings are an attempt to make sense of these gentle reminders.

title: There We Would Now Have Been
description: Platforms: The Teachers Among Us invited emerging and mid-career artists to nominate senior artists who have mentored, taught, or profoundly influenced their artistic journey. Following a citywide nomination and adjudication process, 20 senior artists were selected to create new works to be showcases across civic art platforms. These pieces reflect the importance of mentorship and the intergenerational relationships that helped shape Vancouver’s vibrant art scene.
statement: Ino and Melicertes Tumbling into the Sea, Hermit playing the violin, Pool in the Riesengebirge, Expulsion from the garden of Eden. The ‘Ego Tunnels’ are named for philosopher of mind Thomas Metzinger’s theories that describe human consciousness as a ‘phenomenal tunnel' - a low-fi projection by which we drill our way through an inconceivably rich and complex reality. I’m interested in how this speaks to the hallucinatory nature of human consciousness in it’s often fraught relationship to reality. And in particular how the Romantic’s invented ‘nature’ in the face of unprecedented extraction and commodification.

title: Spa:l' (Raven)
locationOnSite: Southwest corners of the building on the 6th, 12th, and 16th floors.
description: Three Raven sculptures in different poses leaning out over the Southwest corners of the building on the 6th, 12th, and 16th floors.
statement: The Raven (Spa:l'), a significant figure in Musqueam culture, is a powerful transformer. Spa:l' symbolizes humour, change in life, and a lightness of being. It is also known as the cultural hero and the trickster, capable of both generosity and greed. Its unpredictable nature means it is regarded with both respect and wariness, adding to its enigmatic charm. Spa:l' is continually looking for things to entertain himself. Call them playful and curious, crafty and cunning; spa;l' is observed misbehaving and never dull. Just like us, every person sees the world in a different way than another. In many Musqueam stories, spa:l' teaches us about life and right from wrong. He symbolizes the change in life, creativity, and humour.
